parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Table 1.1 lists some SI quantities. Complete the table by indicating with a tick ($\checkmark$) which rows are SI base quantities.

Table 1.1

| quantity | base quantity |
| current |  |
| energy |  |
| force |  |
| mass |  |
hints: Hint 1: Think about the seven building blocks of the SI system that cannot be made from anything simpler - which quantities in the table are fundamental and which are made by combining them?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the Seven SI Base Quantities**
You only need to memorise these seven: mass, length, time, current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity. Everything else in physics is built from them.

Step 2: **Sort the Table**
Current ($I$, unit ampere $\text{A}$) and mass ($m$, unit kilogram $\text{kg}$) are in that list of seven, so they get a tick. Energy (joule) and force (newton) can both be broken down into $\text{kg}$, $\text{m}$ and $\text{s}$, so they are derived quantities with no tick.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Use the definition of power to determine its SI base units.

markscheme_points.text:
units of power = $\text{J s}^{-1}$
= $\text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-2}$ / s
= $\text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-3}$

hints: Hint 1: Start from what power means in words - how is power linked to work done or energy transferred and time?
Hint 2: Now break the energy unit down further - what is $1 \text{ J}$ in terms of $\text{kg}$, $\text{m}$ and $\text{s}$, and what happens when you then divide by $\text{s}$?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start From the Definition of Power**
Power is the rate of doing work, so: $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$ This means the unit of power is joule per second: $$1 \text{ W} = 1 \text{ J s}^{-1}$$

Step 2: **Break the Joule Into Base Units**
Work is force x distance, and force is mass x acceleration. So in units: $$1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N m} = 1 \text{ kg m s}^{-2} \times \text{m} = 1 \text{ kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-2}$$

Step 3: **Divide by Time to Get Power**
Now put that back into $\text{J s}^{-1}$: $$\text{unit of } P = \text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-2} \times \text{s}^{-1} = \text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-3}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A light meter is used to measure the intensity of light in a classroom. Daylight is incident normally on the sensor of the meter. The sensor has an area of $2.2\text{ cm}^2$. The reading on the meter is $950\text{ W m}^{-2}$.

Calculate the power of the daylight incident on the sensor.
hints: Hint 1: Look at the units of the meter reading, $\text{W m}^{-2}$ - what does power per square metre tell you about how intensity, power and area are linked?
Hint 2: Check your area units before you multiply - how do you convert $2.2 \text{ cm}^2$ into $\text{m}^2$? Remember $1 \text{ cm} = 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.
Hint 3: Multiply the intensity by the area in $\text{m}^2$ and give your answer to 2 significant figures in watts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Intensity, Power and Area**
Intensity is power arriving per unit area for radiation incident normally: $$I = \frac{P}{A}$$ Rearranged for power: $$P = I \times A$$

Step 2: **Convert Area to SI Units**
The area must be in $\text{m}^2$ to match $\text{W m}^{-2}$. $$A = 2.2 \text{ cm}^2 = 2.2 \times (10^{-2} \text{ m})^2 = 2.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$$ A common slip is to use $10^{-2}$ once instead of squared.

Step 3: **Calculate the Power**
Now substitute: $$P = 950 \times 2.2 \times 10^{-4}$$ $$P = 0.209 \text{ W} \approx 0.21 \text{ W}$$
